manure-cover-savings.formula: open = (daily_manure + wastewater + bedding) x days + area x (net_precip + storm)/12 + area x freeboard/12; roof_saving = area x (net_precip + storm)/12; covered = open - roof_saving; percent_saved = roof_saving / open x 100.
manure-cover-savings.edition: Manure storage covered-vs-open comparison (USDA-NRCS Conservation Practice 313 waste storage facility), by name.
manure-cover-savings.freeAccess: NRCS Conservation Practice Standard 313 is public federal guidance; the engineer or planner governs the actual design.
manure-cover-savings.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
manure-cover-savings.editionNote: The roof saving is the net precipitation and the 25-year, 24-hour storm the open facility must otherwise bank on its own surface. The freeboard is held the same in both cases (a conservatism - a roofed structure can often carry less). The saving is clean rainwater the operation also avoids hauling and land-applying, so the payback is both smaller storage and less spreading. NRCS 313 and the engineer/planner govern - a planning aid, not the engineer of record.

assumptions.name: Roof removes rain
assumptions.value: a roof eliminates the area x (net_precip + storm)/12 term the open facility carries

assumptions.name: Freeboard held equal
assumptions.value: freeboard is kept the same in both cases (conservative; a roofed structure can often carry less)

grain-aeration-airflow.formula: required_cfm = rate_cfm_per_bu x bushels; cooling_hours = 15 / rate_cfm_per_bu (per cooling front).
grain-aeration-airflow.edition: Stored-grain aeration fan airflow (MWPS / university extension; Shedd airflow-resistance curves), by name.
grain-aeration-airflow.freeAccess: The cfm-per-bushel airflow relation and the cooling-front rule are public MWPS / extension results; the fan selection at the design static pressure governs.
grain-aeration-airflow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
grain-aeration-airflow.editionNote: Static pressure rises steeply with grain depth and the fan power grows about four- to fivefold when the airflow rate doubles and about eight- to tenfold when the depth doubles at the same cfm/bu, so a fan sized on cfm/bu alone stalls against back-pressure in a tall bin and the fan curve must be read at the actual static pressure; aeration cooling (0.1-0.25 cfm/bu) is not the same job as natural-air drying (0.5-1.0 cfm/bu). A sizing aid, not a fan selection.

assumptions.name: Airflow bands
assumptions.value: aeration cooling 0.1-0.25 cfm/bu, natural-air drying 0.5-1.0 cfm/bu

assumptions.name: Static-pressure stall
assumptions.value: power grows ~4-5x when the rate doubles and ~8-10x when the depth doubles; read the fan curve at the design static pressure

volumetric-efficiency.formula: 4-stroke theoretical CFM = displacement(ci) * RPM / 3456 (3456 = 1728 * 2 revs per intake cycle); 2-stroke uses /1728. VE% = actual / theoretical * 100.
volumetric-efficiency.edition: Classical four-stroke airflow derivation; SAE engine-test conventions, by name.
volumetric-efficiency.freeAccess: The 3456/1728 constants are pure unit derivations, public.
volumetric-efficiency.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
volumetric-efficiency.editionNote: Single-derivation; VE above 100% is legitimate for forced induction / tuned runners (not clamped). CFM is at standard density.

assumptions.name: Cycle constant
assumptions.value: 4-stroke fires every 2 revolutions (3456 = 1728 in3/ft3 * 2)

point-load-bearing.formula: A_req = P / (Fc_perp * Cb); required bearing length = A_req / width; actual f_c_perp = P / (width * provided_length).
point-load-bearing.edition: Per the National Design Specification (NDS) for Wood Construction - compression perpendicular to grain and the bearing-area factor Cb, by name; Fc-perp values user-supplied.
point-load-bearing.freeAccess: AWC publishes the NDS free read-only at awc.org; the IBC-adopted edition governs.
point-load-bearing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
point-load-bearing.editionNote: IBC-adopted NDS edition governs; Cb applies only to bearings under ~6 in not near a member end. Does not check crushing of the supported member.

assumptions.name: Fc-perp
assumptions.value: allowable compression perpendicular to grain, user-supplied by species/grade

off-grid-battery.formula: usable_Wh = daily_Wh * days_autonomy; nameplate_Wh = usable_Wh / (DoD * round_trip_efficiency * temperature_derate); nameplate_Ah = nameplate_Wh / system_V.
off-grid-battery.edition: IEEE 1013 (Sizing Lead-Acid Batteries for Stand-Alone PV Systems); IEEE 1561 (PV / Hybrid Power Systems).
off-grid-battery.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
off-grid-battery.editionNote: Single-edition (IEEE 1013 / 1561 stand-alone PV battery-sizing practice; DoD and temperature-derate defaults from manufacturer data. NEC Article 706 governs the installation, not this sizing estimate).

assumptions.name: Usable depth-of-discharge
assumptions.value: about 0.50 for flooded lead-acid; about 0.80 for LFP

assumptions.name: Round-trip efficiency
assumptions.value: about 0.85 lead-acid; about 0.95 LFP

screw-conveyor.formula: Q (ft^3/hr) = (pi/4)(D^2 - d^2) x pitch x RPM x loading x 60, all in feet; mass rate = Q x bulk density.
screw-conveyor.edition: CEMA Screw Conveyor standard (Book No. 350) capacity method, by name.
screw-conveyor.freeAccess: CEMA-published; the swept-volume capacity relation is public. CEMA and the manufacturer govern.
screw-conveyor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
screw-conveyor.editionNote: Single-edition (geometric swept-volume capacity; the trough loading fraction is per the CEMA material class and is user-supplied).

assumptions.name: Loading fraction
assumptions.value: per the CEMA material class (light ~30-45%, heavy/abrasive lower); user-supplied

refrigerant-charge.formula: Line-set charge (oz) = sum over line sections of oz_per_ft(refrigerant, line diameter) x section length; lb = oz / 16. Per-foot values from manufacturer line-set tables (oz/ft). The factory charge and any rated-length credit come from the unit's data plate and are not included.
refrigerant-charge.edition: Manufacturer line-set bulletins (Daikin, Carrier, Trane, Rheem) by name.
refrigerant-charge.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.

assumptions.name: Per-foot adder table
assumptions.value: data/hvac/charge-per-foot.json

mortar-mix.formula: Bag yields per PCA / NCMA: 1 bag (94 lb Type N) yields ~3.0 ft³ mortar; joint volume from joint_thickness × wall_area_per_bag; brick / 8-inch CMU joint-thickness adjustment.
mortar-mix.edition: PCA (Portland Cement Association) Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures by name; ASTM C270 mortar specs by name.
mortar-mix.freeAccess: PCA / ASTM licensed; engineering-practice yield values free in published trade references.
mortar-mix.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

assumptions.name: Mortar type yield
assumptions.value: Type N: 94 lb bag → 3.0 ft³ per PCA Table

plate-cost.formula: Plate cost = Σ (ingredient EP cost × portion size). Suggested menu price = plate cost / target food-cost % (typical 28-32% in casual dining, 22-28% fine dining). Contribution margin = price − plate cost.
plate-cost.edition: Engineering-practice food-cost benchmarks (NRA / National Restaurant Association published industry medians) by name; USDA FoodData Central for ingredient costs when bundled.
plate-cost.freeAccess: NRA Restaurant Industry Forecast free at restaurant.org.
plate-cost.governance: The thermometer on the food is the verdict. Local health department governs.
plate-cost.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice cost-control benchmarks; refresh as menu prices and ingredient costs shift).

assumptions.name: Default target food-cost %
assumptions.value: 30% unless user supplies (casual-dining median per NRA)

base-converter.formula: Positional-notation base conversion. parseInt(value, source_base) -> integer; integer.toString(target_base) -> output. Bases 2 through 36 (limit of JavaScript radix support).
base-converter.edition: Standard positional-notation conversion. The 2-36 range is the upper limit of the [0-9] + [A-Z] digit alphabet.
base-converter.governance: Estimate only. Readability formulas and similar metrics are derived from a representative population and have known edge-case noise. The classroom teacher governs final text selection, grade placement, and assessment decisions.
base-converter.editionNote: The tile handles signed integers up to JavaScript's safe-integer range (2^53 - 1). Fractional / floating-point base conversion is not supported. Negative numbers are converted by sign-magnitude (not two's complement).

assumptions.name: Integer-only
assumptions.value: no fractional support

assumptions.name: Sign
assumptions.value: sign-magnitude (a leading minus prefix is preserved)

assumptions.name: Safe range
assumptions.value: absolute value below 2^53; larger numbers lose precision

working-space-110-26.formula: depth from Table 110.26(A)(1) by nominal voltage to ground and Condition 1/2/3 (0-150 V: 3/3/3 ft; 151-600 V: 3/3.5/4 ft; 601-1000 V: 3/4/5 ft); width = max(30 in, equipment width); headroom = 6.5 ft, with a 90-degree door swing.
working-space-110-26.edition: Working space about electrical equipment, NEC 2023 110.26(A), and dedicated equipment space 110.26(E), by name.
working-space-110-26.freeAccess: NEC is free to read at nfpa.org/freeaccess. Condition 1/2/3 describe what is across from the live parts; the width is the greater of 30 in or the equipment width.
working-space-110-26.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
working-space-110-26.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow NEC 2023. NEC 2026 is the current published edition; jurisdictions on NEC 2017 / 2020 / 2023 / 2026 use slightly different ambient corrections and ampacity ranges; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ.

assumptions.name: Depth table
assumptions.value: 0-150 V to ground is 3 ft for all conditions; 151-600 V is 3 / 3.5 / 4 ft and 601-1000 V is 3 / 4 / 5 ft for Conditions 1 / 2 / 3

assumptions.name: Width and headroom
assumptions.value: width is the greater of 30 in or the equipment width; headroom 6.5 ft or equipment height; a 90-degree door swing is required

heat-treat-soak-time.formula: through-heat = rate x section thickness; soak = rate x section thickness; total at temperature = the sum; charge heat = weight x specific heat x (soak - start); furnace input = charge heat / (through-heat hours x furnace efficiency).
heat-treat-soak-time.edition: The section-thickness soak convention used in heat-treating practice (through-heat and soak each proportional to the maximum section, commonly about one hour per inch at temperature), by name, with charge heat from the sensible-heat relation and the furnace's overall efficiency applied to the input. THIS SPECIFIES NO HEAT TREATMENT: temperature, soak, quench, temper, and properties come from the steel's specification and the applicable process standard. The metallurgist governs.
heat-treat-soak-time.freeAccess: A thickness rule stated as a convention with its rate entered by the user, plus a sensible-heat calculation; no process specification or property table is reproduced.
heat-treat-soak-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
heat-treat-soak-time.editionNote: Soak time is governed by section thickness, not by weight, and that is the single most useful thing to know before loading a furnace. A given weight of thin bar and the same weight of thick bar are entirely different soaks, because what has to happen is that the center of the thickest section reaches temperature and then stays there long enough for the transformation to complete. The common rule of roughly an hour per inch of section at temperature is a convention with a great deal of process-specific variation behind it, and it is separate from the time it takes to get the part hot in the first place, which is why both terms belong printed separately. The thickness leverage is the lesson: doubling the section doubles both terms for a charge that may weigh exactly the same. In heat treating, geometry beats weight every time. The energy side sizes the furnace and the circuit, and the surprise is usually how much of the input never reaches the work, since wall losses, opening losses, atmosphere, and fixturing consume a large share and an overall efficiency well under three quarters is common on a batch furnace. What this cannot do is specify the treatment. The austenitizing temperature, the soak, the quench medium, the temper, and the resulting properties come from the steel's own specification and the applicable process standard, and they depend on the alloy, the prior condition, the required hardness and toughness, and the section size.

assumptions.name: Thickness, not weight
assumptions.value: the center of the thickest section governs; doubling the section doubles both terms

assumptions.name: The hour-per-inch rule is a convention
assumptions.value: process-specific variation is large and the specification governs

assumptions.name: Most of the input is lost
assumptions.value: wall, opening, atmosphere, and fixturing losses put batch-furnace efficiency well under three quarters

slab-dowel-schedule.formula: dowels_per_joint = floor((joint_length_ft x 12 - 2 x edge_clearance_in) / dowel_spacing_in) + 1; total_dowels = dowels_per_joint x num_joints; dowel_diameter_in ~ slab_thickness_in / 8 (advisory).
slab-dowel-schedule.edition: Slab-on-grade load-transfer dowel detailing (ACI 302.1R Guide for Concrete Floor and Slab Construction; ACI 360R design of slabs-on-ground), by name; the dowel size/length/spacing table and the engineer of record govern.
slab-dowel-schedule.freeAccess: The dowel count is public first-principles (one per spacing plus one); the ACI 302 dowel size, length, and spacing come from its detailing table and the structural drawings.
slab-dowel-schedule.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
slab-dowel-schedule.editionNote: Load-transfer dowels are smooth, round, greased (bond-broken) bars set across a construction or contraction joint in a slab-on-grade so that a wheel load crossing the joint is shared between the two panels (they deflect together), while the joint is still free to open as the concrete shrinks -- the dowels slide in their greased or sleeved half. This is fundamentally different from a deformed, fully bonded reinforcing bar carrying shear friction across a structural interface, which is bonded on both sides and does not permit movement. Along a joint the dowels are placed at a uniform spacing, commonly 12 inches on center, held back a clearance from each slab edge, so the count is floor((joint length in inches minus twice the edge clearance) divided by the spacing) plus one for the starting dowel: a 40-foot joint at 12 inches on center with 6-inch edge clearance takes 40 dowels, and five such jointed lines need 200. The dowel diameter is roughly the slab thickness divided by 8 -- about 3/4 inch for a 6-inch slab -- and the dowel is typically about 18 inches long with only ONE end greased or capped so the joint can open on that side; however, ACI 302.1R tabulates the recommended dowel diameter, length, and spacing as a function of slab thickness, and that table (with the structural drawings) governs over the diameter-equals-thickness-over-eight approximation used here for a first estimate. Correct alignment is critical: the dowels must be parallel to the slab surface and to each other, held by a dowel basket or careful placement, because a misaligned (skewed or tilted) dowel locks the joint against movement and cracks the slab. A material-takeoff and detailing aid; the structural drawings, ACI 302 / ACI 360, and the engineer of record govern the dowel size and schedule.

assumptions.name: Dowel count
assumptions.value: dowels per joint = floor((joint length x 12 - 2 x edge clearance)/spacing) + 1; total = per joint x number of joints

assumptions.name: Size advisory
assumptions.value: diameter ~ slab thickness/8, ~18 in long, one end greased; ACI 302.1R gives the size/length/spacing table (governs); align parallel (basket) or the joint locks and cracks

fatigue-safety-factor.formula: Goodman 1/n = sa/Se + sm/Sut; Soderberg 1/n = sa/Se + sm/Sy; Gerber n sa/Se + (n sm/Sut)^2 = 1; Langer ny = Sy/(sa + sm); governing = min(n, ny).
fatigue-safety-factor.edition: The modified-Goodman, Soderberg, and Gerber fluctuating-stress fatigue criteria with the Langer first-cycle-yield line (Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design; Juvinall, Engineering Considerations of Stress, Strain, and Strength), by name.
fatigue-safety-factor.freeAccess: The three fatigue criteria and the Langer line are standard published machine-design results; the corrected endurance limit Se, the strengths, and the stresses are the designer's inputs.
fatigue-safety-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fatigue-safety-factor.editionNote: The infinite-life fatigue safety factor for a uniaxial fluctuating stress with alternating amplitude sigma_a and mean sigma_m. Modified Goodman 1/n = sa/Se + sm/Sut is the standard design line; Soderberg 1/n = sa/Se + sm/Sy is the most conservative (it never yields); Gerber n sa/Se + (n sm/Sut)^2 = 1 is the least conservative and the best fit to test data. Se is the CORRECTED endurance limit (Se' ~= 0.5 Sut for steel with Sut < 200 ksi, times the Marin surface/size/load/temperature/reliability factors) and is taken as an input so the tile needs no material tables. The Langer line ny = Sy/(sa + sm) catches first-cycle yielding, which can govern at high mean stress; the reported governing factor is the smaller of the two. With sigma_m = 0 (fully reversed) every criterion gives n = Se/sigma_a. Uniaxial stress, infinite life; Se from the Marin factors is endurance-limit-marin and finite life is fatigue-finite-life, notch Kf is fatigue-notch-sensitivity, and combined bending, axial, and torsion is fatigue-combined-loading. A design aid; Shigley / Juvinall and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Criteria
assumptions.value: Goodman/Soderberg/Gerber fatigue lines + Langer first-cycle yield

assumptions.name: Endurance limit
assumptions.value: Se is the corrected (Marin-factored) endurance limit, taken as an input

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: uniaxial, infinite life; notch Kf, finite-life S-N, and multiaxial combination are separate

coil-length.edition: The coil / roll stock length annulus identity, first-principles; the coil OD, core ID, and thickness come from the material.
coil-length.freeAccess: The coil-length relation is a first-principles geometric identity (annulus cross-section = length x thickness); the coil OD, core diameter, and material thickness come from the coil.
coil-length.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
coil-length.editionNote: Coil / roll stock length from the annulus identity. The wound material, seen end-on, is an annulus of area pi/4 (OD^2 - ID^2); unwound it is a strip of the same cross-section = length x thickness, so L = pi (OD^2 - ID^2) / (4 t), with OD the coil outside diameter, ID the core (mandrel) diameter, and t the material thickness in the same units. Halving the thickness doubles the length wound to the same coil OD. It is exact for a tightly wound coil with no air gaps or telescoping; the usable length runs slightly short after the last wrap and the core stub. A layout aid; weigh or measure-off to confirm before a critical cut.

assumptions.name: Annulus identity
assumptions.value: wound cross-section pi/4 (OD^2 - ID^2) equals unwound length x thickness

assumptions.name: Tight coil
assumptions.value: assumes no air gaps or telescoping between wraps

assumptions.name: Usable length
assumptions.value: the last wrap and core stub trim the usable length slightly

interpass-temperature-control.formula: T(t) = ambient + (start - ambient) x exp(-t / tau); time to fall from T1 to T2 = tau x ln((T1 - ambient) / (T2 - ambient)). The idle allowance runs from the current temperature down to the preheat minimum; the required wait runs from the current temperature down to the restart temperature, and is zero when the joint is already at or under the interpass maximum.
interpass-temperature-control.edition: Newtonian cooling of a weld joint toward ambient, applied to the preheat-minimum and interpass-maximum window the welding procedure specification sets, by name. The time constant is a property of the specific joint and is MEASURED, not bundled. The WPS and a measured joint temperature govern.
interpass-temperature-control.freeAccess: First-order cooling is public physics; the window limits come from the reader's own procedure and the time constant from their own measurement.
interpass-temperature-control.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
interpass-temperature-control.editionNote: Preheat and interpass are a single window rather than two separate rules, and the welder lives inside it. Below the preheat minimum the hydrogen cracking risk rises and the procedure is violated; above the interpass maximum the cooling time stretches, grain growth costs toughness, and the procedure is violated in the other direction. Both limits come from the welding procedure specification and neither is negotiable in the field. The two outputs answer the two questions that actually arise on a heavy weldment. The idle allowance is how long a welder can stop -- for a fit-up, for a grind, for a break -- before the joint drops below preheat and has to be reheated, and it is usually shorter than people expect, which is why heavy weldments get blankets and why a torch stays lit next to the work. The required wait is the other case, where a pass ran hot and welding cannot resume until the joint comes down, and on a multi-pass joint that wait multiplies into hours of lost production if it happens every pass. The time constant is a property of the specific joint -- its mass, its section, its exposure -- and it must be measured rather than assumed; timing one cooling interval with a contact pyrometer gives it, and the whole schedule follows from that one measurement.

assumptions.name: One window
assumptions.value: preheat minimum and interpass maximum are two ends of the same window, both from the WPS

assumptions.name: Time constant is measured
assumptions.value: tau belongs to the specific joint's mass, section, and exposure; time one cooling interval with a contact pyrometer

assumptions.name: First-order cooling
assumptions.value: exponential approach to ambient; a joint under a blanket or in wind has a different tau

ellipsoid-volume.formula: a=L/2, b=W/2, c=H/2; V = (4/3) pi a b c = pi L W H/6; half-ellipsoid = V/2. Equal axes -> sphere (4/3) pi r^3.
ellipsoid-volume.edition: The ellipsoid volume V = (4/3) pi a b c - standard solid geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
ellipsoid-volume.freeAccess: Pure solid geometry, public; the three axis lengths are user-supplied measurements.
ellipsoid-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ellipsoid-volume.editionNote: Volume of an ellipsoid - the oblong, egg-like solid of an oval or elliptical tank, a stretched dome, or an ellipsoidal float - V = (4/3) pi a b c = pi L W H/6, with the three semi-axes a = L/2, b = W/2, c = H/2 from the full axis lengths L (long), W (wide), and H (tall). When the three axes are equal it becomes a sphere, (4/3) pi r^3. The half-ellipsoid, V/2, is an oval dome (a standard 2:1 dished head is its special case D, D, D/2), so the tile reports it too. Volume is reported in cubic feet and US gallons for a takeoff or a fill. A partial fill to a depth, the surface area (no elementary closed form), and an offset or truncated ellipsoid are separate. A takeoff aid; verify against the drawing.

assumptions.name: Ellipsoid volume
assumptions.value: V = (4/3) pi a b c = pi L W H/6, a/b/c the semi-axes

assumptions.name: Limits
assumptions.value: equal axes give a sphere; half-ellipsoid is a dished head/dome

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: full/half volume; partial fill, surface area, and truncated shapes are separate

annulus-area.formula: ring area = (pi/4)(D^2 - d^2) = pi(R^2 - r^2); outer = (pi/4) D^2; bore = (pi/4) d^2; wall = (D - d)/2. d=0 -> full circle.
annulus-area.edition: The annulus (ring) area (pi/4)(D^2 - d^2) - standard plane geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
annulus-area.freeAccess: Pure plane geometry, public; the outer and inner diameters are user-supplied measurements.
annulus-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
annulus-area.editionNote: Area of a flat annulus (the ring between two concentric circles): ring = (pi/4)(D^2 - d^2) = pi(R^2 - r^2), the outer circle minus the hole. It is the metal cross-section of a pipe or tube (the number you multiply by the material density for weight per length, or by the allowable stress for tension capacity), the face area of a washer, gasket, or ring flange, and the area of a circular border or track. The bore area (pi/4) d^2 is the flow area, and the wall thickness is (D - d)/2. When d = 0 it is a full circle. An eccentric ring, a partial (sector) ring, and the volume of a tube (ring area x length) are separate. Plane figure only. A shop and layout aid; verify critical dimensions on the work.

assumptions.name: Ring area
assumptions.value: (pi/4)(D^2 - d^2) = outer circle minus the bore

assumptions.name: Pipe metal
assumptions.value: the ring is the pipe/tube metal cross-section; bore is the flow area

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: concentric flat ring; eccentric/sector rings and tube volume are separate

circular-arc.formula: Radius R = (chord^2 / 4 + rise^2) / (2 x rise); central angle = 2 x acos((R - rise) / R); arc length = R x angle. The rise is the sagitta (middle ordinate) at midspan.
circular-arc.edition: Circular arc from a chord and rise (the sagitta / middle-ordinate relation) - first-principles circle geometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
circular-arc.freeAccess: Pure circle geometry, public; the chord and rise are user-supplied field measurements.
circular-arc.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
circular-arc.editionNote: First-principles geometry. Valid for minor and major arcs (rise greater than the radius is a major arc); reproduce the curve by swinging the radius from the center or by trammel/string-line.

assumptions.name: Chord and rise
assumptions.value: the chord (span) and the perpendicular rise at midspan are user-supplied measurements of the same arc

reserve-capacity-amp-hours.edition: BCI / SAE J537 reserve capacity, by name; the battery's published rating and a load test govern.
reserve-capacity-amp-hours.freeAccess: The 25 A / 10.5 V / 80 F reserve-capacity definition is a published BCI / SAE J537 rating basis; the reserve minutes come from the battery spec.
reserve-capacity-amp-hours.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
reserve-capacity-amp-hours.editionNote: BCI / SAE J537 reserve capacity is the number of minutes a fully charged 12 V battery at 80 F can deliver 25 A before the terminal voltage falls to 10.5 V; the amp-hours at that reserve rate are 25 x RC/60. This RC-rate capacity is smaller than the 20-hour-rate amp-hours printed on a deep-cycle label, because a higher discharge current delivers less capacity (Peukert's effect), so the two figures are not interchangeable. Cold reduces the available capacity further. A comparison aid, not a substitute for the battery's published rating and a load test.

assumptions.name: Reserve rate
assumptions.value: 25 A draw to a 10.5 V cutoff at 80 F on a 12 V battery

guard-handrail-check.formula: guard required where surface_height > 30 in; min guard 36 in residential (34 in on a stair) / 42 in commercial; max infill 4.0 in (4.375 in on a residential stair); stair handrail 34-38 in. Each measured value is compared to its limit; a 200 lb concentrated load applies regardless.
guard-handrail-check.edition: IRC 2021 (International Residential Code) Section R312 (guards) / R311.7.8 (handrails) and IBC 2021 Section 1015 by section; dimensional minimums only, not reproduced.
guard-handrail-check.freeAccess: Read-only at codes.iccsafe.org. The dimensional minimums are facts; the AHJ-adopted code and edition govern.
guard-handrail-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
guard-handrail-check.editionNote: Multi-edition (the AHJ-adopted IRC / IBC edition governs the guard, handrail, and infill minimums; the 200 lb concentrated load applies regardless).

assumptions.name: Thresholds
assumptions.value: guard over 30 in surface; 36 in residential (34 in on a stair) / 42 in commercial height; 4 in sphere infill (4-3/8 in on a residential stair); 34-38 in handrail

assumptions.name: Load
assumptions.value: guards and handrails must also resist a 200 lb concentrated load in any direction (IRC R301.5 / IBC 1607); this tool checks dimensions only

assumptions.name: AHJ governs
assumptions.value: the AHJ-adopted code and edition govern the final acceptance

smooth-bore-diameter-for-flow.formula: bore_in = sqrt( target_gpm / (29.7 x sqrt(nozzle_pressure_psi)) ), the inverse of gpm = 29.7 x bore_in^2 x sqrt(NP); companion nozzle reaction = 1.57 x bore_in^2 x NP.
smooth-bore-diameter-for-flow.edition: IFSTA Pumping Apparatus Driver/Operator Handbook smooth-bore discharge form (by name), solved for the diameter; classical orifice discharge, no edition cycle.
smooth-bore-diameter-for-flow.freeAccess: The discharge relation is public physics; standard nozzle pressures are 50 psi handline / 80 psi master. Incident command and the pump operator govern.
smooth-bore-diameter-for-flow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
smooth-bore-diameter-for-flow.editionNote: Single-edition (the classical smooth-bore discharge form gpm = 29.7 d^2 sqrt(NP) does not roll; the standard 50 / 80 psi nozzle pressures are editable), solved for the tip diameter a target flow needs. Round to a stocked tip size; the nozzle reaction is reported so the crew can check handling.

assumptions.name: Discharge coefficient
assumptions.value: the 29.7 constant bundles the standard smooth-bore discharge coefficient and unit conversion; the tip must be a true smooth bore

assumptions.name: Nozzle pressure
assumptions.value: default 50 psi handline / 80 psi master, editable to the tip in use

assumptions.name: Estimate
assumptions.value: a discharge estimate; incident command governs the flow target and the pump operator sets engine pressure

ridge-cap-fasteners.formula: cap_len_lf = ridge_lf + hip_lf; cap_bundles = ceil(cap_len_lf / cap_lf_per_bundle); field_nails = squares x shingles_per_sq x nails_per_shingle; cap_pieces = ceil(cap_len_lf x 12 / cap_exposure_in); cap_nails = cap_pieces x 2; total_nails = field_nails + cap_nails; nail_lbs = ceil(total_nails / nails_per_lb).
ridge-cap-fasteners.edition: IRC R905.2.6 (asphalt-shingle fastening: at least four nails per strip shingle, and the manufacturer's count where it is higher; six in the manufacturer's high-wind / steep-slope instructions) and the shingle manufacturer's application instructions, by name; the cap-bundle and nail relations are first-principles arithmetic.
ridge-cap-fasteners.freeAccess: The fastening pattern is stated in the published IRC R905.2.6; the cap-bundle and nail relations are public roofing-takeoff arithmetic. The cap coverage and nails-per-shingle are the product wrapper's values.
ridge-cap-fasteners.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ridge-cap-fasteners.editionNote: IRC R905.2.6 sets a floor of four nails per strip shingle and defers to the manufacturer, whose high-wind and steep-slope instructions call for six; the shingle manufacturer's application instructions govern the product. The nails-per-shingle and the cap coverage per bundle come from the product's wrapper and the adopted wind zone (a pre-formed hip-and-ridge product covers far less per bundle than field-cut three-tab caps); the shingles-per-square is the product's count. A material takeoff, not a fastening approval.

assumptions.name: Cap bundles
assumptions.value: cap length = ridge + hip; cap bundles = ceil(cap length / lf per bundle): a pre-formed hip/ridge product (~20 lf) covers far less per bundle than field-cut 3-tab (~35 lf)

assumptions.name: Field nails
assumptions.value: field nails = squares x shingles per square x nails per shingle: IRC R905.2.6 sets a floor of four nails per strip shingle; the manufacturer's high-wind / steep-slope instructions call for six

assumptions.name: Nails by the pound
assumptions.value: cap pieces = ceil(cap length x 12 / exposure), two nails each; nail lbs = ceil(total nails / nails per pound): roofers order nails by the pound, not the each

rc-punching-shear.formula: bo = 2(c1 + d) + 2(c2 + d) interior, 2(c1 + d/2) + (c2 + d) edge, (c1 + d/2) + (c2 + d/2) corner (c1 perpendicular to the edge); beta = max(c1,c2)/min(c1,c2); vc = min(4, 2 + 4/beta, 2 + alpha_s d/bo) x lambda_s x lambda x min(sqrt(f'c), 100), lambda_s = min(sqrt(2/(1 + d/10)), 1.0); phi Vc = 0.75 vc bo d. (alpha_s = 40/30/20 interior/edge/corner)
rc-punching-shear.edition: The ACI 318-19 Table 22.6.5.2 two-way (punching) shear stress (least of the three terms) on the 22.6.4.1 critical section at d/2 from the column face, with alpha_s = 40/30/20 and phi = 0.75, by name.
rc-punching-shear.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; Table 22.6.5.2 and the 22.6.4.1 critical-section definition are in the published code.
rc-punching-shear.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rc-punching-shear.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 Table 22.6.5.2 two-way shear stress as the least of 4 lambda sqrt(f'c), (2 + 4/beta) lambda sqrt(f'c), and (2 + alpha_s d/bo) lambda sqrt(f'c), each times the 22.5.5.1.3 size-effect factor lambda_s = min(sqrt(2/(1 + d/10)), 1.0) with sqrt(f'c) capped at 100 psi (22.5.3.1), the d/2 critical perimeter, alpha_s = 40/30/20 for an interior/edge/corner column, and phi = 0.75. This returns the concrete two-way shear capacity on the d/2 critical section for a rectangular column - it assumes shear without unbalanced-moment transfer (no gamma_v eccentric-shear amplification), no shear reinforcement or shear-cap/drop panel, and a rectangular column; the edge column takes a three-sided perimeter and the corner column a two-sided one, with the slab edge flush with the column face. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Critical section
assumptions.value: the perimeter bo at d/2 from the column faces; capacity phi vc bo d

assumptions.name: Three-term least
assumptions.value: 4, 2 + 4/beta, and 2 + alpha_s d/bo, each x lambda sqrt(f'c); the least governs

assumptions.name: Position constant
assumptions.value: alpha_s = 40 interior, 30 edge, 20 corner

erv-total-enthalpy-recovery.formula: Q = 4.5 x CFM x effectiveness x (h_outdoor - h_return); h_supply = h_outdoor - effectiveness x (h_outdoor - h_return).
erv-total-enthalpy-recovery.edition: The energy-recovery-ventilator total (enthalpy) recovery relation (ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals / AHRI 1060 effectiveness), by name.
erv-total-enthalpy-recovery.freeAccess: The 4.5 x CFM x effectiveness x enthalpy-difference total-recovery relation is a standard published air-side result; the effectiveness is the AHRI 1060 rating.
erv-total-enthalpy-recovery.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
erv-total-enthalpy-recovery.editionNote: ERV total (enthalpy) recovery: Q = 4.5 x CFM x the total-energy effectiveness x (the outdoor-air enthalpy - the return/exhaust-air enthalpy) Btu/hr (4.5 = 60 x 0.075 standard air), and the air leaving the wheel toward the space has an enthalpy = h_outdoor - effectiveness x (h_outdoor - h_return). In summer the outdoor air carries more energy than the return, so the wheel pre-cools and dries the ventilation air (a positive Q, offloading the cooling coil); in winter it pre-warms and humidifies it (a negative Q). The effectiveness is the AHRI 1060-rated total-energy value at the design airflow. Feed the two enthalpies from moist-air-enthalpy. This returns the recovered energy and the supply state; it does not add the fan energy or the frost-control penalty. A design aid; the ERV manufacturer's rated effectiveness governs.

assumptions.name: Total recovery
assumptions.value: Q = 4.5 x CFM x effectiveness x (h_oa - h_ra)

assumptions.name: Supply state
assumptions.value: h_supply = h_oa - effectiveness x (h_oa - h_ra)

assumptions.name: Rated effectiveness
assumptions.value: the AHRI 1060 total-energy effectiveness at design airflow

equipment-heat-load.formula: sensible_btu_hr = total_equipment_watts x 3.412; required_cfm = sensible_btu_hr / (1.08 x target_temp_rise_f); temp_rise_at_exhaust = exhaust_cfm > 0 ? sensible_btu_hr / (1.08 x exhaust_cfm) : null.
equipment-heat-load.edition: Watt-to-heat conversion (3.412 BTU/hr per watt) and the 1.08 standard-air sensible-heat relation, by name; ANSI/IICRC S500. Field-arithmetic identities, not edition-bound.
equipment-heat-load.freeAccess: The watt-to-heat conversion and the 1.08 sensible relation are public HVAC arithmetic; the efficient-evaporation band is named in the published IICRC S500.
equipment-heat-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
equipment-heat-load.editionNote: Single-edition (the conversion and sensible relation do not roll). Every watt of equipment draw becomes sensible heat (3.412 BTU/hr per watt); the 1.08 factor is 60 min x 0.075 lb/ft^3 x 0.24 BTU/lb-degF for standard air. An overheated chamber leaves the efficient-evaporation band and drives secondary damage and microbial growth. Envelope losses and the building HVAC GOVERN the real number; this is a screen. ANSI/IICRC S500 names the band.

assumptions.name: Standard air
assumptions.value: the 1.08 sensible factor assumes standard air (0.075 lb/ft^3, 0.24 BTU/lb-degF); altitude and temperature shift it

assumptions.name: All draw becomes heat
assumptions.value: essentially every watt the chamber's equipment draws lands in the room as sensible heat

expansion-guide-spacing.formula: first_guide = d1_mult x pipe_od (default 4 diameters from the joint); second_guide = d2_mult x pipe_od (default 14 diameters past the first guide); guide 2 is first_guide + second_guide from the joint.
expansion-guide-spacing.edition: The Expansion Joint Manufacturers Association (EJMA) 4-diameter / 14-diameter guide-placement rule and the manufacturer installation guides, by name.
expansion-guide-spacing.freeAccess: The 4D/14D first-and-second-guide rule is the EJMA published placement standard, republished in every manufacturer's installation guide.
expansion-guide-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
expansion-guide-spacing.editionNote: The 4D/14D rule places the first TWO guides; intermediate guide spacing beyond the second guide comes from the EJMA table or the pipe-column stability calc (user-supplied / manufacturer), and the anchor and joint selection govern. This places the planning guides, it does NOT design the anchor loads.

assumptions.name: First two guides
assumptions.value: first guide within 4 pipe diameters of the joint, second within 14 diameters of the first

assumptions.name: Beyond guide 2
assumptions.value: intermediate guide spacing comes from the EJMA table or a pipe-column stability calc (user-supplied)

assumptions.name: Anchors
assumptions.value: the anchor loads and joint selection are a separate design and govern

baghouse-cleaning-interval.formula: working range = trigger pressure minus the clean-bag baseline; the baseline rise against an earlier log is the blinding diagnostic, and at the observed rate the months until the baseline reaches the trigger is the remaining range over that rate; pulses per day = operating hours x 60 / the cycle time.
baghouse-cleaning-interval.edition: Fabric filter cleaning practice as baghouse operation states it -- a healthy collector cycles between a stable clean-bag BASELINE and its cleaning trigger, and a rising baseline means the cake is not releasing (blinding), which is irreversible; the trigger sets the peak, so the peak shows nothing. On-demand cleaning by differential pressure is preferred over timer cleaning. Pressures and cycle times are ENTERED from the plant's own log. It does not compute pressure drop from air-to-cloth ratio and dust loading, predict or diagnose blinding, size the pulse system, or evaluate emissions.
baghouse-cleaning-interval.freeAccess: Two pressures and a cycle time from the plant's own log.
baghouse-cleaning-interval.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
baghouse-cleaning-interval.editionNote: The BASELINE is the diagnostic and the peak is not, because the trigger sets the peak: a collector whose baseline has climbed shows an unchanged peak the entire time. What has changed is the working range, which shrinks from one end, so the cycle shortens and the collector pulses more often -- and that shortening is visible on any cleaning log even where the baseline was not recorded. Over-cleaning is the opposite error and it is what timer cleaning produces: it removes the residual cake that does most of the fine filtration, emissions rise briefly after each pulse, the fabric is flexed more often and fails sooner, and compressed air is spent for nothing.

assumptions.name: Pressures are entered
assumptions.value: this reads a log rather than modelling the collector

assumptions.name: Blinding is detected, not predicted
assumptions.value: its causes are moisture, a sticky dust, or operating below the gas dew point

assumptions.name: No emissions estimate
assumptions.value: a pulse briefly raises outlet loading and that is not modelled

sand-permeability-vent.formula: green sand steam volume from the ideal gas law PV = nRT (R = 10.7316 ft^3 psi per lbmol degR, water 18.0153 lb per lbmol) at the entered pouring temperature and one atmosphere, plus binder gas = binder mass x an entered evolution rate in cm3 per gram; permeability is scaled with the SQUARE of grain size.
sand-permeability-vent.edition: Foundry mould gas estimation. spec-v1715 supplied no arithmetic of its own, so only relations that can be defended from first principles are computed and everything else is stated as guidance. The binder gas evolution rate is ENTERED because binder suppliers publish it in cm3/g and it differs by binder system and by the metal poured against it.
sand-permeability-vent.freeAccess: The ideal gas law and one published binder rate.
sand-permeability-vent.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sand-permeability-vent.editionNote: Water expands roughly seventeen hundred times on flashing at the boil and nearly eight thousand times at pouring temperature, so a sand a percent or two over its target moisture generates gas faster than any permeability can pass it -- a problem no venting and no sand change fixes, because the control is at the MULLER. CORES ARE THE WORST CASE and are not in this arithmetic: a core is surrounded by metal on nearly every side, its binder decomposes as soon as metal arrives, and its only escape is through its own body to its prints, so an unvented core or one whose prints seal sends that gas into the casting, and the blowholes appear on the cored surface where inspection is hardest. The permeability trade does not resolve in general, which is why a foundry runs more than one sand system.

assumptions.name: Volumes, not rates
assumptions.value: whether a casting gases depends on the RATE against the mould's passing rate

assumptions.name: Binder gas rate is entered
assumptions.value: differs by binder system and by the metal poured

assumptions.name: Gas per vent area is comparative
assumptions.value: a ranking figure against a mould that ran sound, not an acceptance criterion

effective-leakage-area.formula: ELA (US, 4 Pa reference) = CFM50 / 18.2 in square inches, and EqLA (Canadian, 10 Pa reference) = CFM50 / 10.0; specific leakage area = ELA / floor area, both in the same units (square feet), so it is dimensionless; normalized leakage = 1000 x SLA x (building height / 8.2 ft)^0.3, which for real houses runs about 0.1 to 1.5 (ASHRAE 119 classes A to J). The hole side is the square root of the ELA.
effective-leakage-area.edition: The LBL effective leakage area conversion at the 4 Pa reference and the CGSB equivalent leakage area at 10 Pa, both by name, with the ASHRAE Fundamentals normalized-leakage definition and its height correction. The two conventions describe the SAME building and differ by reference pressure AND discharge coefficient (1.0 US, 0.61 Canadian), so a figure quoted without its convention cannot be compared with one quoted under the other.
effective-leakage-area.freeAccess: Two published divisors and one power-law height correction.
effective-leakage-area.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
effective-leakage-area.editionNote: The point of the conversion is communication rather than physics: 102 square inches is a hole about 10 inches on a side, permanently open in the envelope, and that sentence changes a homeowner's mind where an ACH50 figure does not. The trap is the CONVENTION -- the US and Canadian figures for one building differ by about 1.8x, and comparing an ELA against an EqLA reports a difference that does not exist. Normalized leakage carries the height correction that ACH50 lacks, which is why two houses with the same ACH50 can have quite different real air change rates and why normalized leakage rather than ACH50 is the right basis for estimating natural infiltration.

assumptions.name: Reference pressure
assumptions.value: 4 Pa for ELA, 10 Pa for EqLA

assumptions.name: Height correction exponent
assumptions.value: 0.3 about an 8.2 ft reference

assumptions.name: Same units
assumptions.value: ELA converted to square feet before dividing by floor area; spec-v1495 mixed square inches with square feet and read 144 times high

assumptions.name: Single-zone envelope
assumptions.value: the model does not say where the leakage is

pump-impeller-trim.formula: trim affinity: Q2/Q1 = D2/D1, H2/H1 = (D2/D1)^2, P2/P1 = (D2/D1)^3; the required diameter is the current one times the flow ratio, or, for a throttled pump at unchanged flow, times (required head / current head)^(1/3) (DOE Pumping Systems Tip Sheet #7); the head at the trimmed diameter is checked against the head required; and the annual saving is the motor power times one minus the power ratio, over the operating hours.
pump-impeller-trim.edition: The impeller-trim affinity relations as pump practice writes them, noting that a TRIM is not a speed change: it alters the impeller's geometry relative to its casing, so the correspondence is APPROXIMATE and the manufacturer's published trim curves are the authority. The practical limit of roughly 75 to 80% of the casing maximum is ENTERED. It does not read a pump curve, compute efficiency at the trimmed condition, check NPSH available, or address minimum flow.
pump-impeller-trim.freeAccess: Three affinity ratios and one energy calculation.
pump-impeller-trim.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pump-impeller-trim.editionNote: A pump throttled to reduce flow develops head the system does not need and destroys it across a balance valve, converting power directly into water temperature. A trimmed impeller never develops the excess head at all, so the saving persists for the life of the pump with no control action. Because power goes as the CUBE of the diameter ratio, a modest trim is a large power reduction. Two checks decide whether the trim is usable and both are computed rather than left as caveats: the trimmed pump must still make the required HEAD at the required flow, and below roughly three quarters of the casing maximum the efficiency falls off and the affinity estimate itself becomes unreliable.

assumptions.name: The trim relations are approximate
assumptions.value: trimming changes geometry relative to the casing, unlike a speed change

assumptions.name: No efficiency at the trimmed point
assumptions.value: efficiency falls as the tip-to-casing gap grows

assumptions.name: NPSH is not checked
assumptions.value: the new operating point has its own requirement

subgrade-cbr-thickness.formula: cover thickness = alpha x sqrt( wheel load x ( 1/(8.1 x CBR) - 1/(pi x tire pressure) ) ), with the coverage factor alpha = 0.23 log10(coverages) + 0.15; resilient modulus Mr = 1,500 x CBR; the geosynthetic value is that thickness reduced by an entered percentage.
subgrade-cbr-thickness.edition: The Corps of Engineers CBR cover equation by name, with the widely used Mr = 1,500 x CBR correlation, which is reasonable for fine-grained soils at low CBR and drifts above about CBR 10. NO COVER CHART IS SHIPPED; agency charts differ between the construction-platform and pavement-design cases. The geosynthetic thickness reduction is ENTERED from the manufacturer's design method. The geotechnical investigation, the agency's design manual, and the geotechnical engineer govern.
subgrade-cbr-thickness.freeAccess: One square root and one logarithm on a CBR the reader measures; no agency cover chart is reproduced.
subgrade-cbr-thickness.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
subgrade-cbr-thickness.editionNote: Cover falls steeply as CBR rises, so measuring the subgrade rather than assuming it is worth a great deal: assuming CBR 5 on ground that tests at 2 produces a section that pumps and ruts before the first winter. Traffic enters only as a logarithm, so a haul road carrying ten times the passes needs about a quarter more rock rather than ten times as much. The sensitivity is computed rather than asserted because it is routinely overstated -- going from CBR 3 to CBR 10 at a fixed wheel load cuts the rock by about half, not by four. Below about CBR 3 the calculation still returns a thickness and the subgrade deforms under construction traffic anyway; that is an undercut, a stabilization, or a designed working platform, and this says so.

assumptions.name: A screening estimate, not an agency chart
assumptions.value: charts differ between agencies and between platform and pavement cases

assumptions.name: CBR is a crude index
assumptions.value: sensitive to moisture and compaction at the time of testing; a summer value is not a spring value

assumptions.name: The geosynthetic reduction is entered
assumptions.value: it must come from the manufacturer's design method and the specification

daily-cover-volume.formula: cover volume = working face area x cover depth; its share = cover volume / (waste airspace + cover volume); the airspace value = cover volume x the committed cost per cubic yard.
daily-cover-volume.edition: Geometry against the site's own airspace value. Six inches of daily cover is the common baseline requirement; the permit and the regulator govern.
daily-cover-volume.freeAccess: Public arithmetic; the requirement itself is in the site's permit.
daily-cover-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
daily-cover-volume.editionNote: The cover is doing a job -- vector, litter, odour, fire, and scavenging control -- and an alternative daily cover has to be APPROVED as meeting those purposes before any of this saving is available.

assumptions.name: Airspace value
assumptions.value: the committed cost per cubic yard, before the cost of buying, hauling, and placing the soil

assumptions.name: Alternative cover
assumptions.value: its own annual cost is entered and netted; approval is not assumed

pipe-freeze-time.formula: per foot: C = water lb/ft x 1.0 + pipe lb/ft x cp; UA' = 1 / (ln(r_out / r_pipe) / (2 pi k) + 1 / (h x 2 pi r_out)); t1 = (C / UA') x ln((T_start - T_amb) / (32 - T_amb)); t2 = water lb/ft x 143.5 / (UA' x (32 - T_amb)); onset t1 and solid t1 + t2 reported as bounds, with the bare pipe for comparison.
pipe-freeze-time.edition: Steady radial conduction through the insulation and an outside surface film, a lumped cool-down of the water and pipe wall, and the latent heat of fusion of water (143.5 Btu/lb) by name, with the ASHRAE Handbook -- Fundamentals chapter on insulation for mechanical systems cited by name for the freeze-time approach. Conductivity and surface coefficient are entered; the insulation manufacturer's data governs.
pipe-freeze-time.freeAccess: Textbook conduction and a latent-heat balance on the user's own pipe and insulation dimensions; no ASHRAE table or manufacturer chart is reproduced.
pipe-freeze-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
pipe-freeze-time.editionNote: Insulation slows a freeze and prevents none. Half an inch of foam on a 3/4 in copper line cuts the heat loss per foot by about three-fifths and roughly multiplies the time by two and a half, but still water in an unheated crawl space at a hard-freeze temperature reaches 32 degF within about an hour and is solid within a working day. Freezing takes longer than cooling because water gives up 143.5 Btu per pound to become ice, more than a hundred times what it gave up per degree on the way down. The onset and the solid time are bounds: where a pipe blocks or splits depends on where the ice forms and how pressure builds behind it. Keeping water moving, by a dripping faucet, is what prevents a freeze; draining the line is what prevents the burst. Heat from the structure or the soil, wind, and supercooling are not modeled.

assumptions.name: Still water, one pipe run
assumptions.value: no flow, no heat from the structure or soil, no supercooling

assumptions.name: Latent heat of fusion of water
assumptions.value: 143.5 Btu/lb

assumptions.name: Water density
assumptions.value: 62.4 lb/cu ft for the water in the pipe
